items.article: CIOs aren’t replacing key enterprise IT systems with their own vibe-coded software. The industry is facing upheaval anyway. The SaaSpocalypse is real but perhaps a little exaggerated. CIOs and corporate software buyers are threatening vendors with vibe-coding, but it’s much more about getting a better price than it is about actually switching. The idea is appealing: get an agent to replicate your existing solution and run it in-house for a few hundred dollars in tokens and ditch the costly software license agreement. Never talk to another software salesperson again. So far, it’s not working. Yet. One survey showed that 35 percent of teams have replaced at least one enterprise application with something they vibe-coded, but this is most often in categories like workflow automation and business analytics—these are additions and don’t point to actually cancelling the entire software license. Industry revenue retention—the rate at which customers renew—has fallen slightly, but there’s no agreement on the cause and earnings haven’t been significantly affected. Having a vendor is useful because the true cost of vibe-coding software is much higher than a few hundred dollars in tokens. items.article: A Colorado man's unusual commute to work is catching the attention of tens of thousands online. Jake Hutzler, an air traffic controller, travels to his job site at Pueblo Memorial Airport by power paragliding at least once a week and shares his flying adventures on Instagram. "There's nothing better than flying to work, you know, 500 feet in the air, sipping your coffee," Hutzler told ABC News' Danny New . While he's soaring through the sky, Hutzler says he likes to sip coffee and even eat breakfast, like a burrito. The father of one said paragliding from his home to the airport takes about the same time as driving a car -- about 20 minutes, but if he catches a good tailwind, he can shave his travel time down to 15 minutes or less. "It's probably the closest thing that you can get to a jetpack," said Hutzler. To power paraglide, Hutzler wears an engine propeller backpack called a paramotor, which can typically cost between $8,000 and $9,000.

items.article: Nikhitha Swaminathan and Aanya Jindal won the Grade 7-9 ExploraVision title for a passive heat-control concept aimed at electronics, data centres and spacecraft. Their project turns a classroom idea into national recognition while tackling a real engineering challenge with future applications. Their regional achievement was celebrated at Lowery Freshman Center, with Toshiba's John Ausmus joining Principal Jill Stafford and House Principal Moriah Ahlfinger to recognise the students. The result marked the biggest milestone yet for the pair, who finished first in the Grade 7-9 division. At the centre of the students' project is a problem faced by engineers across several technology sectors: how to move and manage heat efficiently. Their proposed micro-gap thermal diode is designed as a passive approach to heat control. Instead of depending on conventional active cooling systems, the concept focuses on controlling heat flow through a specialised structure. The students identified possible applications in electronics, data centres and spacecraft, all of which face demanding thermal-management challenges. Data centres, for instance, generate significant heat as computing systems operate continuously, making thermal management important for maintaining performance and reliability. Spacecraft face a different set of challenges, with equipment having to operate within tightly controlled thermal conditions.

items.text: Missing The Volume Slider On Your iPhone Lock Screen? Here Is How To Bring It Back
items.article: Apple hid the iPhone lock screen volume slider in iOS 16 and later brought it back as a hidden setting. Here is how to turn it on in a few taps. If you listen to music or podcasts on your iPhone, you may have noticed that the lock screen no longer shows a volume slider. Apple removed it with iOS 16 in 2022, leaving users to rely on the physical volume buttons, which change the volume in fixed steps. The slider has since returned as an option, but Apple has placed it in Accessibility settings, where many users never look. The physical buttons on the side of an iPhone raise or lower the volume in set increments. This can leave you stuck between a level that is slightly too loud and one that is slightly too quiet. The on-screen slider lets you make finer adjustments with your finger, without unlocking the phone. It is especially handy when your iPhone is propped up on a desk, lying on a bedside table or mounted in a car. How to enable the volume slider on your iPhone lock screen You will need iOS 18.2 or later. The setting is also available in newer versions of iOS.
